surface: audit log append, rotation and check
boundary: SHA-256 hash chain with head recorded in the vault file (R28, R29)

local_checks.invariant: append serializes writers, chains each line to the hash of the previous line across rotation, never overwrites a rotated file, and flushes before a use (R28)
local_checks.result: append_line holds an flock on a separate lock file for the read-last-line, rotate and write sequence. Rotation refuses an existing target name and opens the new log with create_new. prev continues from rotated_head when the new log is empty. The text hashed is exactly the serialized line, and serde_json escapes newlines in caller fields. Server::record maps an append failure to AuditUnavailable, so the use is refused.

local_checks.invariant: check proves the chain from genesis through every rotated file and requires the head recorded in the authenticated vault file to appear in it (R29); an edited, deleted or reordered line before that head is reported
local_checks.result: walk verifies line.prev == the running head for every line from GENESIS and rejects non-UTF-8 or unparseable lines. Rotated files checked earlier are pinned by dev, inode, length, mtime and ctime stamps, and a mismatch triggers a full check. full_check returns AuditHeadMissing unless the recorded head is found, and holds() accepts GENESIS only as the recorded value, which only a key holder can write. commit appends the line before saving the head. A full check runs at daemon start and on `audit --all`. The remaining gaps are hardening against a same-UID writer who could rewrite the vault file with the readable key anyway: lines after the last change can be truncated, and the incremental check does not re-read the already-checked prefix of the current audit.log.

Every commit and renew raises the generation (src/vault.rs:297, 912), so this is reachable only after a million changes. Fix: sort by the parsed generation_of() value, or zero-pad to 20 digits.

Files with this vault's prefix and a higher generation, written into iCloud Drive by another device on the same account, would outrank the real copies: the mirror would delete each real backup right after copying it and still report ok. Anyone who can write the synced folder can already delete files there, and the report is stated as unverified. Hardening: prune the mirror only among names that match files the mirror copied from the local folder, or use the local folder's generation set.

The vault key never rotates and the AAD (magic+id) carries no generation, so an older vault.bin decrypts. audit::check accepts any earlier head still in the chain, and needs_backup passes because that generation's backup matches. The next commit then finds the existing future backup for N+1, fails with BackupMismatch, and ready_for_change refuses all later changes. Only a same-UID writer can do this. Checking doc.generation against the newest local backup's generation at open would turn this into a clear alarm.

vault::restore (src/vault.rs restore) accepts any backup whose payload.recovery_recipient matches the typed identity, and it does not bind to the recovery recipient of the restore point that `vault reset` left. It also does not re-validate restored records (validate_name, rule parse, caps.validate, kind/field consistency). While no vault is open (after reset, or after `install --for-restore`), a same-UID process can install a vault under its own recovery key first. Binding a file restore to the recipient recorded beside the restore point, and re-running record validation on restore, would close this. It is not a finding because the attacker is same-UID.

Audit chain (src/audit.rs): with an unkeyed chain and the head saved only at changes, a same-UID writer can drop use lines written after the last change without detection. The incremental check() also only reads past the checkpoint offset of the current audit.log, so an in-place edit of an already-checked line shows up only at the next daemon start or `vault audit --all`. Both are within the accepted same-UID trade-off. Recording a periodic head, or stamping the current file's checked prefix, would narrow them.

keyprotect::load falls back to the plain vault.key when unsealing the TPM credential fails and both files exist (an interrupted seal). Status reports it, but a disk copy taken in that state opens the vault anywhere. Finishing or retrying the seal at daemon start would shorten that window.
